sentences: Red horses and straining men surge as one mass, as if about to burst out of the frame.
Standing before this canvas, three metres wide, you feel the dust and shouting first.
Take a moment to feel its momentum.
The Italian painter Umberto Boccioni made this in 1910, and it is counted as his first major Futurist work.
The artists of Futurism celebrated machines, labour and the fast-growing city.
This painting turns that belief into a picture, almost like a manifesto.
First, look along the very top.
Buildings wrapped in scaffolding and factory chimneys stand in a hazy row.
This is a new city under construction on the edge of town, going up before our eyes.
At the centre, a huge red horse hurls its body forward.
Its dark blue harness slashes across the red flank, driving diagonally down through the picture.
This horse is a symbol of the energy and speed that the modern city carries within it.
Move to the right, and you find a bridled horse's head and a rope pulled taut.
The men cling to the reins, yet the horse drags them forward instead.
It is a tamed beast still straining against its tethers.
Below, men twist and brace themselves against the pull.
Arms and legs blur like afterimages, and a black hoof-like shape kicks off the ground.
You see motion itself before you see any figure.
On the left, beside a white horse, a man with raised arms staggers.
The men clinging on are so entangled that you cannot tell whether they are dragged or running along.
Human and animal force all lean one way.
Look closely at the red horse, and you will see long, thin strokes splitting like threads.
Colours sit side by side instead of being blended, so the whole surface seems to vibrate.
Even so, the buildings and a sense of perspective remain.
Here Boccioni traded the calmer suburban views of his earlier work for a swirling, charged surface.
Its original title was Il lavoro, or Work, and it hung under that name at the Exhibition of Free Art in Milan in 1911.
The composer Ferruccio Busoni bought it in Berlin in 1912, when the Futurist exhibition toured there, and the Museum of Modern Art acquired it in 1951.
Boccioni himself died in 1916, aged thirty-three, after being thrown from his horse during cavalry training.
Finally, step back and ask: is the horse leading the men, or are the men holding the horse back?
The picture never says plainly whose strength is raising this new city.
